reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of intestinal protein digestion caused by TMPRSS15 variants affecting enteropeptidase (enterokinase)
Enteropeptidase normally activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which in turn activates other pancreatic proteases, so its loss disables the proteolytic cascade
Infants present with diarrhoea, failure to thrive, hypoproteinaemic oedema and sometimes anaemia due to protein maldigestion
Pancreatic architecture and lipase and amylase activity are normal, but luminal protease activity is markedly reduced
Duodenal aspirate shows low trypsin activity that increases substantially when exogenous enteropeptidase is added, confirming the defect
The clinical picture can mimic generalised pancreatic insufficiency but is confined to protein digestion
Pancreatic enzyme substitution corrects maldigestion and reverses the failure to thrive and oedema
reference.pathophysiology: Enterokinase deficiency arises from loss-of-function variants in TMPRSS15, which encodes the duodenal brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase. Enteropeptidase is the physiological activator of trypsinogen, cleaving it to active trypsin, which then activates the remaining pancreatic zymogens including chymotrypsinogen and proelastase. Without enteropeptidase this activation cascade fails, so dietary protein is poorly digested despite normal pancreatic secretion of enzyme precursors. The resulting protein maldigestion causes chronic diarrhoea, hypoproteinaemia with oedema and impaired growth, while fat and carbohydrate digestion remain comparatively intact.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic fibrosis and other causes of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
Cow's milk protein and other food-protein enteropathies
Other congenital diarrhoeal disorders with failure to thrive
additionalInvestigations: Duodenal aspirate protease activity before and after adding exogenous enteropeptidase
Serum total protein and albumin to assess hypoproteinaemia
Faecal elastase and other markers to distinguish from generalised pancreatic insufficiency
Molecular genetic testing for TMPRSS15 variants
Nutritional assessment including anaemia workup and growth monitoring
redFlags: Severe hypoproteinaemia with generalised oedema in an infant
Marked failure to thrive from protein maldigestion
Diagnostic confusion with pancreatic insufficiency leading to inappropriate management
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent once recognised, as pancreatic enzyme substitution restores protein digestion, reverses oedema and hypoproteinaemia and allows normal growth. Some tolerance of protein may improve with age.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as global pancreatic insufficiency without noting normal fat digestion
Overlooking hypoproteinaemic oedema as a clue to protein maldigestion
Failing to perform the enteropeptidase activation test on duodenal fluid
Attributing the picture to a protein-losing enteropathy without assessing digestion
